### 2026-10-18 â€“ What I did this session

**4.63h**

What I did this session

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cS9KscHhpXWpAjsHTuU1VWQAnI2MBiQy/7e03b22fd38b9d48a4c12b6611e03fa4cd52d2d878b65ab9f383f6f2c657f661.png)
**Goal: get the flexi world map actually modeled in Onshape, from a blank document, on recording.** This session was basically 30% modeling and 70% recovering from my own bad measurements â€” but that's the session honestly.

### First attempt: the strip ratio disaster

Started recording and went straight into making the first strip without properly planning the ratio. I took the strip width as **4 cm** â€” sounded fine in my head â€” but when I ran the math for the full 40 cm trail, that width gave me barely any strips. The whole map was going to be like 10 tiles wide, which is not a world map, that's a Lego. The ratio between strip width and total length was just wrong.

I let it run for a while trying to patch it (scale here, stretch there) before accepting that **patching a bad base measurement is a trap** â€” every downstream feature inherits the error. So I killed it, rolled back to the original version, and started from scratch. That restart cost me maybe an hour of recording time but it was the right call.

### Second attempt: planned before I sketched

This time I did the boring thing first â€” wrote down the numbers **before** touching a single sketch tool:

- strip width: **1 cm each**
- slit between strips: **2 mm**
- everything else dimensioned off those two

Immediately everything clicked. The strip count actually made sense for the 40 cm length, and the 2 mm slits are exactly the right gap for the hinge to live in. Lesson I basically already knew from the KiCad week: measure first, model second. Ask me how many times I have to relearn it.

### The copy-paste hell

Assembling the strips was the worst part. My first instinct was **linear pattern** â€” which in theory is the right tool, but in practice I was fighting it every step: the instance count, the spacing, the direction, one wrong reference and the whole array lands somewhere in space. I wasted a lot of time nudging pattern parameters when what I actually wanted was to just lay each strip down.

So I **got rid of the linear pattern entirely** and went old-school: paste and position, strip by strip. It's more manual, it's slower, but every piece ends up where I actually put it and I can see errors immediately instead of discovering them later in a broken array.

## The map scale problem

When the actual world map got involved: **the file came in at a totally wrong scale** â€” way too large. The transform tool was another major haul, because the map is the feature that everything else (strips, slits, borders) has to align to. Rescaling it meant re-checking every reference. I ended up pulling in **Gemini to help me work through it**, which got me moving again. Not ashamed â€” the tool is a tool.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cS9KscHhpXWpAjsHTuU1VWQAnI2MBiQy/6ea513075584962f3cea1ca755c060fdaca841d9fcbd4e1d1f23b8db4d034c77.png)

### Where it ended up

By end of session: **the map is at correct scale, strips are 1 cm with 2 mm slits, and the layout is fully planned and executable.** Nothing fancy yet â€” no hinge geometry, no color split â€” but the skeleton is right, which is the part that would have ruined the print if I'd gotten it wrong.

### 2026-10-19 â€“ I actually finished it. (a day late, and it nearly killed me)

**3.0h**

Let me get the embarrassing part out of the way first: **today is October 19th. Week 2 ended yesterday.** I'm filing this because the last stretch of this project broke me a little and I refused to go to sleep with it unfinished. The last 3+ hours are on the timelapse and honestly they were the worst ones. i got the base layer done before â€” 1cm strips, 2mm slits, all planned out. then came the actual world map and it just. broke me.

the DXF hellscape. i downloaded SO many world map files and almost all of them were unusable. some were just lines â€” outlines with no closed shape so you can't extrude them into anything. some were literal dots?? opened the file and it was just a scatter of points like a printer having a seizure. some were all fused together so you'd select africa and get the entire atlantic along with it. and some had incomplete loops â€” the coastline would just stop, leave a gap, pick up somewhere else. a continent shaped like a broken moon.

for a bunch of those i actually had to draw the coastlines by hand. like close the loops myself in the sketcher. if you've never traced coastline by coastline at midnight it's this weird hypnotic soul-crushing thing. at one point i genuinely considered abandoning the map and just making a flexi rectangle and calling it abstract art. i did not. (i thought about it a LOT.)

eventually found one good file â€” a .txt of all things â€” that imported clean with actual closed shapes. i have no idea why the universe made the good one a text file. i was beyond asking questions by then.

then the real problem showed up. my base had the 2mm slits right, but the map layer had extruded as one solid slab. no slits at all. so it was just sitting on the base like a rug over a venetian blind â€” holding the whole thing stiff. which kills the entire point of the project. the flexi part. the rolling part. gone.

fixing it took forever because i could not explain it properly to gemini. i kept going back and forth â€” no the slits need to go through the map too, no wait not through, it just needs to be divided at the slit lines, no actually maybe through â€” and getting back a different wrong model each time. i was describing geometry with my hands at a monitor at 1am. we got there in the end: make the slits in the map solids the same way, then boolean union the whole thing into one part. slits line up, hinge lives, one flexible piece off the plate. i still don't know why that took 3 hours.

colors ended up as wood for the base and this chocolatey coffee brown for the map and it genuinely looks better than i planned?? it reads like an old explorer map that's been in someone's pocket for a century.

the map itself is not cartographically perfect. some coastlines are irregular, an island might be chunky. i know. i stared at them for hours. it stays â€” it's a map, not a navigation instrument.

in case my hours get questioned: the 3h in the lapse are real. scrub it and you'll watch the same map get imported, break, get hand-fixed, and re-imported like a dozen times. that's the work. it's late. it's done. and i'm going to sleep.

**What worked:** not quitting at the broken-map stage. the boolean union.
**What didn't:** every world map file on the internet, apparently, and my ability to describe boolean operations at 2am.
